relationship: Solomon rules in parallel royal openings
rationale: Kings names Solomon reigning over Israel; Chronicles opens with Solomon son of David growing strong over his kingdom. The corresponding royal subject and rule are retained without adding a date to either opening.

relationship: Same-chapter The roster possessive receives its named royal antecedent
rationale: The officials notice begins with his officials and Azariah son of Zadok; the preceding unit identifies King Solomon over Israel. This identifies whose roster follows without adding the title priest to Azariah's actual entry.

relationship: Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud has the recorder role in both rosters
rationale: Both rosters explicitly name Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud as recorder. Kings separately names Elihoreph and Ahijah son of Saba as scribes; those names are not substituted for Samuel's other officials.

relationship: The named Zadok-Abiathar priest pair recurs
rationale: Both units explicitly call Zadok and Abiathar priests. The comparison follows those named roles without importing a new chronology or changing the other officials in either roster.

relationship: Same-chapter The overseer entry is read with the appointed-officer function
rationale: Ornia son of Nathan is over the appointed officers, while the following heading gives the officers' monthly provision for Solomon's household. Zabud's separate companion role is not merged with that provisioning office.

relationship: Adoniram appears with the levy and tribute administration
rationale: The roster names Adoniram son of Ephra over tributes; the later shift account names Adoniram over the levy. The stated duties and patronymic are preserved without substituting a differently named official.

relationship: Monthly household provision is subsequently described in operation
rationale: The heading assigns Solomon's appointed officers one month each to provide for king and household; the later account describes their monthly table provision. The additional horse-feed duties in that later unit remain its own details.

relationship: Same-chapter Benor in Ephraim’s hill country
rationale: The Benor entry assigns Ephraim's hill country; the list heading supplies the appointed officers' purpose of monthly provision for the king and household. No new tribal ancestry or altered personal name is inferred.

relationship: Same-chapter The son of Rechab and his named district
rationale: The son of Rechab is assigned the actual Machemas-to-Beth-hanan district; the heading explains the roster's monthly provisioning function. Its place forms remain unchanged rather than being replaced with familiar equivalents.

relationship: Same-chapter The son of Esoth and the district assignment
rationale: The son of Esoth is listed with Berbethnema, Lousamencha and Rhesphara; the heading defines the listed office through provision for the royal household. The connection is list membership and function, not independently solved geography.

relationship: Same-chapter The marriage-bearing entry belongs to the appointed-officer list
rationale: The entry names Chinanadab, Anaphathi and Tableth with the Solomon-daughter marriage clause; the heading identifies the officers' provisioning function. Its difficult personal forms and pronoun assignments are not independently rewritten.

relationship: Same-chapter Baccha’s named multi-place assignment follows the officer heading
rationale: Baccha son of Ahilud is assigned Taanach, Megiddo and the remaining supplied places; the heading explains the monthly royal provision attached to the roster. This does not equate every place form with another book's spelling.

relationship: Sixty fortified cities associated with Bashan in different accounts
rationale: Kings assigns Geber's son Eregaba's Bashan district with sixty great walled cities and bronze bars; Deuteronomy reports sixty cities of Og's Bashan kingdom with walls, gates and bars. The Eregaba/Argob forms and bronze detail are not independently harmonized.

relationship: Same-chapter Ahinadab’s Mahanaim assignment receives the stated office function
rationale: Ahinadab son of Achel is assigned Mahanaim within this roster; the heading states that the appointed officers provide for Solomon and his household by month. His assignment is not independently mapped to a modern location.

relationship: Same-chapter Ahimaaz’s district and marriage notice occur within the provisioning list
rationale: Ahimaaz is assigned Naphtali and is said to have married Basemath, Solomon's daughter; the heading gives the listed officers' monthly provision role. The marriage does not replace the stated administrative function.

relationship: Same-chapter Baana’s Maalath entry is governed by the roster’s stated function
rationale: The entry names Baana son of Hushai in Maalath; the heading explains the monthly provision for the royal household. It supplies that function without independently identifying Hushai with another named companion.

relationship: Same-chapter Shammah’s Benjamin entry belongs to the appointed-officer enumeration
rationale: Shammah son of Elah is listed in Benjamin; the preceding heading states the officers' purpose and monthly responsibility. The connection does not invent further district boundaries or another name for Shammah.

relationship: Gad and the Sihon-Og kingdoms occur in the territorial descriptions
rationale: The Geber entry places Gad's land in the lands of Sihon and Og; Numbers includes Gad among recipients of those two kingdoms. The different administrative and distribution contexts, and Numbers' other recipient groups, remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter Jehoshaphat’s Issachar assignment belongs to the provisioning roster
rationale: Jehoshaphat son of Phouasoud is assigned Issachar; the list heading defines the appointed officers through monthly royal provision. He is not conflated with the differently patronymic recorder in4:3.

relationship: The actual monthly provision recalls the officers’ stated duty
rationale: The officers provide the king's table each in his month; the earlier heading assigns each appointed officer a month to provide for the king and household. The later barley-and-straw statement is not inserted into the heading.

relationship: Same-chapter The daily requirement heading continues into its animal provisions
rationale: The daily list gives thirty kors of fine flour and sixty of pounded meal; the next unit continues with the cattle, sheep and other provisions. The daily heading is not changed into a yearly or monthly ration.

relationship: Same-chapter The animal provisions belong to the explicitly daily royal list
rationale: The calves, cattle, sheep and other named animals continue the requirements introduced as Solomon's needs for one day. This connects the inventory to its actual time scale without inventing a diner count.

relationship: Peace around Solomon corresponds to the stated rest promise
rationale: Kings says Solomon had peace on every side; David's reported divine word in Chronicles names Solomon and promises rest from surrounding enemies and peace in his days. The differing geographical detail is not silently supplied to Chronicles.

relationship: The wisdom-gift account corresponds to the Lord’s stated gift
rationale: Kings reports the Lord giving Solomon discernment and very great wisdom; the earlier divine speech gives him a discerning and wise heart. The sand comparison remains the later narrator's particular description.

relationship: Same-chapter Broad discernment comparisons continue with named exemplars
rationale: The narrator compares Solomon with ancient people and Egypt's discerning people, then says he was wiser than all people and names four men. These are the account's stated comparisons, not a new independent survey of every ancient thinker.

relationship: Same-chapter The named sages occur within the preceding wisdom-comparison sequence
rationale: The named Gaithan, Heman, Calcol and Darda comparison follows the wider comparison with ancient and Egyptian discernment. Their supplied personal forms and sons-of-Mal clause are not equated with another genealogy.

relationship: Solomon’s reported compositions beside a named Solomonic wisdom collection
rationale: Kings credits Solomon with three thousand parables and five thousand songs; Proverbs names Solomon son of David and introduces wisdom sayings and comparisons. This does not claim every counted composition is preserved in that collection or alter either total.

relationship: Same-chapter Named natural subjects follow the counted speech and song report
rationale: The report of Solomon speaking about trees and animal kinds follows the count of his parables and songs. The two notices distinguish counted compositions from named subjects rather than assigning every topic to a particular surviving song.

relationship: Kings hear Solomon’s given wisdom and bring gifts
rationale: The earlier notice has peoples hear Solomon's wisdom and kings bring gifts; the later account explicitly has earth's kings seek his discernment and bring gifts year by year. Their actual scopes and later gift list remain visible.

relationship: Pharaoh’s daughter and the royal-house accommodation notices
rationale: The continuation places Pharaoh's daughter in the City of David until the building projects are finished; the later house account includes a house for the Pharaoh's daughter Solomon married. It does not reconstruct every move or completion date.

relationship: Same-chapter The Pharaoh-daughter gift expands the preceding marriage notice
rationale: Pharaoh gives the captured places as gifts to his daughter, Solomon's wife; the preceding original continuation says Solomon took Pharaoh's daughter as wife. Gezer and Mergab remain the supplied forms without an independently solved site equation.

relationship: Hiram king of Tyre has an explicit earlier David connection
rationale: Hiram king of Tyre sends attendants concerning Solomon and is said to have loved David; Samuel earlier names Hiram king of Tyre supplying David's house. The actual to-anoint wording is not replaced with a different diplomatic purpose.

relationship: Same-chapter The sending notice introduces Solomon’s actual building-and-timber message
rationale: Solomon sends to Hiram, and the following units give the message: David's wars, present rest, the promised son's house and the Lebanon timber request. The introduction is linked to that particular content.

relationship: David’s wars and the stated inability to build the name-house
rationale: Solomon attributes David's inability to build to surrounding wars; David's reported divine word in Chronicles mentions great wars and bloodshed. The source's war explanation is not expanded into every clause of the other reported speech.

relationship: Solomon’s reported surrounding rest beside the earlier promise
rationale: Solomon says the Lord has given rest on every side without a plotter or evil encounter; Chronicles' reported promise names Solomon and rest from surrounding enemies. The present speech and earlier promise remain their own statements.

relationship: The son-building promise is explicitly recalled
rationale: Solomon quotes the promise that David's successor son will build the house for the Lord's name; Samuel's divine speech promises David a succeeding seed who will build that name-house. No additional throne chronology is supplied.

relationship: The Lebanon timber request combines skilled cutters and shared servants
rationale: Solomon requests Lebanon timber and cooperation with Hiram's servants, praising Sidonian skill; Chronicles likewise requests Lebanon timbers because the other servants know cutting. Its cedar, juniper and pine list is not inserted into Kings' unspecific timber request.

relationship: The Tyrian king blesses God for David’s wise son
rationale: Hiram blesses God for giving David a discerning son over the people; Chronicles' Chiram blesses Israel's Lord for David's wise son and his building work. The supplied names and differing additional praise remain unchanged.

relationship: Same-chapter The timber answer responds to the actual cutting request
rationale: Hiram promises to fulfill Solomon's timber wishes with cedar and pine after Solomon requests timber from Lebanon. Cedar and pine are the answer's named materials, not words silently added to the request.

relationship: Lebanon timber is conveyed by rafts in the two replies
rationale: Hiram proposes bringing Lebanon timber to the sea and making rafts to the requested place; Chronicles specifies rafts to Joppa and onward transport to Jerusalem. Kings' unnamed delivery place is not independently replaced with Joppa.

relationship: Same-chapter The cedar supply follows the specific timber promise
rationale: Hiram supplies Solomon with cedars and what he desired after promising cedar and pine. The later notice explicitly names cedars, without separately enumerating every delivered item or timber quantity.

relationship: Twenty-thousand provisioning figures occur in the timber arrangements
rationale: Kings gives Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat and machir and twenty thousand beth of oil yearly; Chronicles lists grain, barley, wine and oil gifts with its own measures. Machir is not silently translated as barley, nor are beth and measures independently equated.

relationship: Wisdom given as promised refers to the actual earlier divine gift
rationale: The narrator says the Lord gave Solomon wisdom as promised; the earlier divine speech gives a discerning and wise heart. The subsequent Hiram-Solomon peace and covenant remain additional statements rather than part of the earlier quoted promise.

relationship: Same-chapter The raised levy receives its stated shift arrangement
rationale: The king raises thirty thousand men from Israel; the next unit posts ten thousand monthly to Lebanon, with one month there and two at home. The actual totals and shift periods are not replaced with a new labor calculation.

relationship: The named levy supervisor recurs in the administrative roster
rationale: Adoniram supervises the Lebanon levy shifts; the earlier roster names Adoniram son of Ephra over tributes. Both offices retain their own labels without changing the patronymic or identifying an otherwise different official.

relationship: The burden-bearer and quarry-worker totals correspond
rationale: Both accounts give seventy thousand burden bearers and eighty thousand workers cutting stone in the mountains. Chronicles also gives the overseers in this unit; Kings states that separate total in its following unit.

relationship: The three-thousand-six-hundred oversight total is stated in both
rationale: Kings numbers the work overseers at three thousand six hundred; Chronicles gives that same taskmaster total with the burden bearers and quarrymen. The count is not replaced with the different familiar three-thousand-three-hundred figure.

relationship: The stone-and-timber preparation precedes the foundation-work notices
rationale: Stones and timber are prepared for three years; the later original continuation units describe carrying foundation stones and Solomon's and Hiram's sons hewing and laying them. Their actual sons wording and the preparation duration remain intact.

relationship: The fourth-year second-month construction dating corresponds
rationale: Kings dates the account to Solomon's fourth year and second month, also giving a four-hundred-fortieth exodus year; Chronicles states fourth year and second month. The absent exodus interval is not supplied to Chronicles or changed to four hundred eighty.

relationship: Costly great foundation stones appear in distinct building descriptions
rationale: The temple foundation notice uses great, costly stones and unhewn stones; the later royal-complex foundation notice gives costly great stones of ten and eight cubits. Those later dimensions are not assigned to the temple stones.

relationship: The hewing-and-laying notice follows material preparation
rationale: Solomon's sons and Hiram's sons hew and lay them in the foundation sequence; the earlier account prepared stones and timber for three years. This follows the stated materials without changing sons into a newly translated workforce label.

relationship: Same-chapter The foundation date repeats the fourth-year second-month dating
rationale: The continuation explicitly dates the foundation to the fourth year and Niso, the second month; the opening likewise names fourth year and second month. Niso is retained rather than replaced with another supplied month name.

relationship: The house-completion notice and the later furnishing closeout remain distinct
rationale: The house is completed in the eleventh year, Baal the eighth month; the later notice concludes Solomon's Lord-house work and stores consecrated objects. Its broader closeout is not independently assigned the earlier building date.

relationship: The house length and width descriptions preserve their different lengths
rationale: Kings gives the house forty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty-five high; Chronicles gives sixty long and twenty wide. The shared width and differing lengths are retained without reconstructing a harmonized plan or adding a Chronicles height.

relationship: The frontage spans twenty cubits across the house’s width
rationale: Kings' porch spans twenty cubits across the house and is ten cubits wide; Chronicles' ailam spans twenty across the house and has its own height. Width and height are not equated or transferred between accounts.

relationship: Concealed windows occur in construction and temple-vision descriptions
rationale: Kings makes recessed concealed windows for the house; Ezekiel's vision mentions concealed windows near the porch ceilings and joined side chambers. The common window feature does not establish an identical building plan or measurement.

relationship: Side chambers around the house are described beside its wall
rationale: Kings places beams against the wall and side chambers all around; Ezekiel measures the house wall and surrounding side chambers with an interval. The vision's dimensions and chamber-number wording are not assigned to Solomon's construction.

relationship: Widening upper chambers and wall intervals occur in both descriptions
rationale: Kings widens the lower, middle and third chambers from five to six to seven cubits and leaves outside space; Ezekiel describes a wall interval and widening upper chambers. Its thirty-and-three twice-over wording is not replaced with a new count.

relationship: Stone construction has differently scoped iron restrictions
rationale: Kings says no hammer, axe or iron implement was heard during the house construction; Deuteronomy forbids laying iron on altar stones. Temple hearing and altar tool-use restrictions remain distinct, and sharply cut unworked is not rewritten.

relationship: Lower-to-middle-to-third-story access is described in both
rationale: Kings describes a winding ascent to the middle tier and then the third story; Ezekiel describes going from lower parts to upper stories and from middle to third. The vision is not given an unmentioned winding stair.

relationship: Coffered house interiors appear with explicit wooden treatment
rationale: Kings furnishes the house with a coffered cedar ceiling; Ezekiel describes coffered, wood-covered areas and carving from floor to coffered ceiling. The vision's wood is not independently identified as cedar.

relationship: Same-chapter The connecting-structure notice adds to the wall-and-chamber construction sequence
rationale: The connecting structures are five cubits high and held with cedar timbers; the earlier notice introduces beams around the house wall and surrounding chambers. These particular construction notices are compared without a new technical identification of every structural term.

relationship: Cedar paneling appears in both house-interior descriptions
rationale: Kings gives cedar timbers from floor upward and pine boards inside; Chronicles panels the great house with cedar and adds gilding and carved palms. Pine is not reassigned only to a floor, nor is gilding inserted into this Kings unit.

relationship: The twenty-cubit inner area is identified as the Holy of Holies
rationale: Kings makes the twenty-cubit end of the house the Holy of Holies; Chronicles names that holy room and its twenty-by-twenty measurements. Its gold quantity is not assigned to Kings' less detailed unit.

relationship: Same-chapter The original split temple description continues into the inner-sanctuary purpose clause
rationale: The forty-cubit temple unit ends in front; the next actual unit continues of the inner sanctuary and states the ark-placement purpose. The missing numbered6:18 is not fabricated to join the source's actual ordered text.

relationship: The intended ark location is later occupied
rationale: The inner sanctuary is prepared to place the covenant ark there; the later account has priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary, the Holy of Holies. This connects stated purpose with the particular narrated placement.

relationship: Gold and the twenty-by-twenty holy-room measurements correspond
rationale: Kings gives twenty cubits each for length, width and height and refined gold; Chronicles gives twenty for the holy room's length and width with gold. Kings' height and its continuing altar clause are not supplied to Chronicles.

relationship: The gold-covered altar reappears in the furnishing inventory
rationale: The altar begun in6:20 is placed before the inner sanctuary and covered with gold in this continuation; the later inventory lists the gold altar. The split source wording is retained rather than merged into an invented verse unit.

relationship: Gold covers the house in both construction summaries
rationale: Kings says the whole house is gold-covered until finished; Chronicles lists gilding of the house, walls, gateways, ceilings and doors. Their different level of detail is preserved rather than making both lists equally exhaustive.

relationship: Two cherubim occupy the innermost holy room
rationale: Kings makes two cherubim in the inner sanctuary; Chronicles makes two in the Holy of Holies. Kings' ten-cubit measure and Chronicles' explicit wooden work and gilding remain their respective additional details.

relationship: Five-cubit cherub wings occur in both descriptions
rationale: Kings measures one cherub's two wings at five cubits each and ten tip to tip; Chronicles gives five-cubit wings in the joined-wing arrangement. Its combined twenty-cubit spread is not substituted for Kings' single-cherub span.

relationship: Same-chapter The second cherub’s matching measure refers to the first wing description
rationale: The second cherub has the same measure and form as the first; the preceding unit gives that first cherub's five-cubit wings and ten-cubit span. This identifies the stated measurement reference without adding an unreported material.

relationship: Same-chapter Equal heights specify the stated matching measure of the pair
rationale: Each cherub is explicitly ten cubits high; the preceding notice says both share one measure and finished form. The height equality does not replace the separately given wing spans.

relationship: Outspread wings touch walls and the other cherub
rationale: Kings spreads the wings to the walls and wing-to-wing in the house's middle; Chronicles describes five-cubit wings touching walls and the other cherub. Its added stance and face direction are not assigned to Kings.

relationship: The inner-room cherubim are gilded
rationale: Kings covers the cherubim with gold; Chronicles expressly gilds the two Holy-of-Holies cherubim. Its wooden-work statement remains an additional detail rather than a material newly inserted into Kings' unit.

relationship: Cherubim and palms are carved on the house walls
rationale: Kings engraves cherubim and palms on the inner and outer walls; Ezekiel's temple vision also carves cherubim and palms from floor to ceiling. The vision's two-faced figures are not added to Solomon's account.

relationship: Same-chapter The golden floor specifies coverage within the earlier whole-house summary
rationale: Kings explicitly gilds the inner and outer floors after saying the whole house was covered with gold. The floor is the particular surface specified here, not an independently measured new room.

relationship: Same-chapter The inner-entry sequence retains both of its actual door-material notices
rationale: The first notice gives juniper-wood doors and fivefold posts; the next gives two pine-wood doors with carvings and gold. Juniper is not silently restricted to frames to erase the different supplied door descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter The two entry accounts repeat the carved cherub-palm-petal motifs
rationale: The pine doors bear cherubim, palms and spreading petals with gold; the later entry relief repeats those same three motifs and gold. The inner and temple entrance contexts remain distinct rather than being one newly identified doorway.

relationship: Same-chapter The temple and inner-entry notices preserve different fourfold and fivefold arrangements
rationale: The temple entrance has juniper posts and fourfold porticoes; the inner entrance earlier has juniper doors and fivefold posts. Their components and counts are not normalized into one common doorway description.

relationship: Two leaves for each pivoting doorway occur in both
rationale: Kings describes two pine doors, each with two turning leaves; Ezekiel's temple vision describes two pivoting doorways with two leaves each. The vision is not assigned Kings' named wood species.

relationship: Cherubim and palms recur on carved temple doorways
rationale: Kings engraves cherubim, palms and petals beneath gold on the entry relief; Ezekiel carves cherubim and palms on the temple doorways. The common motifs do not add Kings' petals or gilding to the vision.

relationship: Three stone courses and one cedar course occur in the court descriptions
rationale: The innermost court uses three courses of unhewn stones and one of worked cedar; the royal-complex great court likewise has three stone courses and one carved-cedar course. The courts are not independently declared the same enclosure.

relationship: Curtain or covering at a sanctuary-court entrance
rationale: Kings builds a curtain for the porch court before the temple; Exodus prescribes a covering for the court gate. The twenty-cubit-high and colored-work details of Exodus are not assigned to Kings' curtain or confused with an inner-sanctuary veil.

relationship: Same-chapter The introduced Hiram later completes the named furnishing work
rationale: Solomon brings Hiram from Tyre; the later inventory names Hiram finishing his works for Solomon in the Lord's house. This follows the artisan narrative without identifying him with the separately titled Hiram king of Tyre.

relationship: Tyrian father and metalworking skill occur with differing maternal notices
rationale: Kings' craftsman has a Tyrian father, bronze skill and a Naphtali notice; Chronicles' Chiram has a Tyrian father, broad craft skills and a mother from Dan's daughters. The Naphtali and Dan clauses are not independently harmonized.

relationship: The eighteen-cubit pillar height recurs in the later object account
rationale: Kings' casting notice gives eighteen-cubit pillars with the second alike; the later account likewise gives eighteen cubits and a matching second pillar. Fourteen-cubit circumference, fingerbreadths and hollowness are not supplied to that later unit.

relationship: Five-cubit capitals are explicitly measured in both
rationale: Both notices give five-cubit capitals on two pillars. Chronicles' thirty-five-cubit pillar height is not substituted for Kings' eighteen-cubit pillar notice, and the shared capital measurement does not erase that difference.

relationship: Two covering networks occur above the two pillars
rationale: Kings makes one net for each pillar capital; Chronicles lists two networks covering the chothareth heads on the two pillars. The particular covering count is shared without independently translating every supplied ornament label.

relationship: Pomegranates are arranged in two rows or groups on the networks
rationale: Kings describes two rows of bronze pomegranates in hanging net work; Chronicles gives two pomegranate groups on each network. Its four hundred golden bells are not silently changed into Kings' differently counted pomegranates.

relationship: Two erected temple pillars receive names in both accounts
rationale: Kings names the two porch pillars Iachoum and Boaz; Chronicles names the right and left pillars Establishment and Strength. The two naming accounts are compared without a newly certified etymology or changed supplied name.

relationship: Same-chapter Lily-form decoration occurs on different bronze furnishings
rationale: Lily-work is placed atop the pillars, while the Sea's cup-like brim is likened to a lily shoot. The recurring named flower form has different positions; the pillar's four-cubit notice is not assigned to the basin rim.

relationship: Same-chapter The beam-capital notice follows the earlier cast-capital description
rationale: A beam over both pillars forms a capital in its thickness; the earlier notice describes two cast-bronze capitals. These distinct formulations are kept without independently giving the beam the earlier capital's five-cubit height.

relationship: The round Sea dimensions share diameter and height but differ in circumference
rationale: Both describe a round Sea ten cubits across and five high; Kings gives thirty-three cubits around and Chronicles thirty. No circumference correction or reconstructed geometric reconciliation replaces either actual number.

relationship: Encircling elements beneath the Sea retain different labels and measures
rationale: Kings has supports beneath the brim at ten to a cubit; Chronicles has encircling calf likenesses and its actual ten-cubits wording. These related below-Sea descriptions do not establish identical objects or a harmonized counting unit.

relationship: The thick cup-like Sea rim is shaped as lily growth
rationale: Both describe the Sea's rim with a cup and lily form, and give palm or handbreadth thickness. Chronicles' three-thousand-metretes capacity is not assigned to Kings' unit, which states no capacity.

relationship: Twelve supporting cattle are grouped three in each stated direction
rationale: Both give twelve cattle in four groups of three beneath the Sea. Kings' toward-the-sea and hindquarters-toward-the-house clauses remain distinct from Chronicles' west and inward clauses rather than being independently normalized.

relationship: Same-chapter The measured stand prototype belongs to the stated common ten-stand pattern
rationale: Kings measures each of ten stands at five by four by six cubits; the following design summary says all ten share one arrangement and measure. Those dimensions are not replaced with another edition's measurements.

relationship: Same-chapter The panel structure receives its specified images in the continuation
rationale: The stands have enclosed panels between projecting parts; the next unit expressly places lions, cattle and cherubim on those panels. The structural description is tied to its actual named decorative surfaces.

relationship: Same-chapter The enclosed-panel image lists share lions and cherubim with different additional motifs
rationale: The first panel description names lions, cattle and cherubim; the later names cherubim, lions and palms. Both lists are retained without adding cattle to the later list or removing palms from it.

relationship: Same-chapter The four bronze wheels receive their stated cast construction description
rationale: The stands have four bronze wheels and attachments; the later unit says the wheels resemble chariot wheels and their arms, backs and assembly are cast. This does not reconstruct an unreported vehicle or axle design.

relationship: Same-chapter The wheel-arm and height notice is read with the cast-wheel construction
rationale: Kings places the wheel arms in the stand and gives a cubit-and-half height; the next unit describes the chariot-like wheels and their cast parts. The height is not independently converted into modern dimensions.

relationship: Same-chapter The cast-wheel account complements the preceding placement and height notice
rationale: The chariot-like wheels have cast arms, backs and assembly; the preceding unit locates their arms in the stand and gives their height. The two particular wheel descriptions are compared without inventing missing mechanical details.

relationship: Same-chapter The shoulder descriptions specify corner unity and a position beneath the basins
rationale: Four shoulders at the stand's corners are one piece with it; the earlier wheel-and-attachment unit also locates shoulders beneath the basins. The common named component is compared without forcing every ambiguous part reference into a new diagram.

relationship: Same-chapter The round upper-part description belongs to the common stand pattern
rationale: The stand has a half-cubit round upper part with arms and panels; the concluding notice gives all ten stands one arrangement and measure. The summary applies the described pattern without inventing a diameter or another shape for half a cubit.

relationship: Same-chapter The later panel imagery preserves the repeated and differing named motifs
rationale: The later enclosed panels show cherubim, lions and palms, while the earlier list has lions, cattle and cherubim. The comparison follows the two actual motif lists rather than declaring every panel identically decorated.

relationship: Same-chapter The shared stand measure recalls the earlier explicit prototype dimensions
rationale: All ten stands share one arrangement and measure; the initial stand notice gives five-cubit length, four width and six height. Those are the source's actual dimensions, not an imported four-by-four-by-three pattern.

relationship: Same-chapter Ten basins on ten stands recur in the furnishing inventory
rationale: The source makes ten bronze basin vessels, one on each stand, and the later inventory repeats ten stands and ten basins. The source's forty-choes capacity is not inserted into that later count-only inventory.

relationship: The Sea is placed at the house’s right toward the east
rationale: Kings places the Sea on the house's right, eastward toward the southern slope; Chronicles places it at the right-hand corner toward the east. Kings' added stand placements and southern-slope clause are not supplied to Chronicles.

relationship: The craftsman’s completed work introduces the furnishing lists
rationale: Hiram finishes his Solomon Lord-house works after naming cauldrons, braziers and bowls; Chronicles' Chiram likewise finishes God's-house work with its own implement list. Different named implements are not independently declared exact lexical equivalents.

relationship: The inventory repeats two pillars and two covering networks
rationale: Both inventories list two pillars with top ornaments and two covering networks. Kings' twisted-ornament wording and Chronicles' golath/chothareth forms remain as given rather than being independently translated into identical technical parts.

relationship: Network pomegranate arrangements preserve a different four-hundred object label
rationale: Kings counts four hundred pomegranates on two nets in two rows; Chronicles counts four hundred golden bells and separately gives pomegranate groups. The shared net decoration does not turn golden bells into pomegranates or certify an object-name equation.

relationship: Ten basin-bearing structures occur in both inventories
rationale: Kings lists ten stands with ten basins; Chronicles makes ten mechonoth with basins upon them. Their support-and-basin arrangement is compared while keeping mechonoth as supplied and not adding a separate basin count to that Chronicles unit.

relationship: The one Sea and twelve animals recur in the summary counts
rationale: Both inventories give one Sea and twelve cattle or calves beneath it. Neither summary is expanded into a new capacity, directional arrangement or metal-weight measurement.

relationship: The named craftsman’s Lord-house objects are explicitly bronze
rationale: Both accounts place the craftsman's utensils for Solomon's Lord-house in bronze. Kings' cauldrons, braziers, bowls and forty-eight-pillar notice retain their own scope, without assigning that pillar count to Chronicles' different implement list.

relationship: Bronze abundance has differently worded weight statements
rationale: Kings says the abundant bronze had no measured weight; Chronicles says the vessels were abundant and the bronze supply by weight did not run out. Unmeasured quantity and continuing supply are not rewritten as one identical statement.

relationship: Casting in the Jordan region and thick earth occurs in both
rationale: Both place the king's casting in the Jordan region in thick earth. Kings' between-Succoth-and-Sira clause and Chronicles' house-of-Sokchoth and Sirdatha wording are preserved without a modern site identification or rewritten geographical syntax.

relationship: The gold altar and bread-bearing table inventory corresponds
rationale: Both list the golden altar and bread-bearing gold table or tables among the Lord-house furnishings. Kings' singular table and Chronicles' plural tables remain their actual wording rather than an imposed common count.

relationship: Golden lampstands are placed five on each side
rationale: Kings places five refined-gold lampstands on each side before the inner sanctuary; Chronicles gives ten golden lampstands, five on each side in the temple. Kings' accompanying gold implements remain additional details.

relationship: Gold implements and inner holy-room doors appear in both inventories
rationale: Both inventories include gold implements and gold doors for the Holy of Holies and temple house. The different utensil lists are not collapsed into new name equations or made an identical exhaustive inventory.

relationship: Completed Lord-house work and David’s consecrated treasure are recorded
rationale: Both conclude the Lord-house work and place David's silver, gold and vessels in its treasury. Kings additionally names Solomon's consecrated things; that added clause is not silently attributed to Chronicles.

relationship: Same-chapter The thirteen-year royal-house notice has its own completion close
rationale: Kings says Solomon built his own house in thirteen years; the chapter later says he completed his entire house. This is the royal-house project, not a substituted duration for the Lord-house chronology.

relationship: Same-chapter The cedar-pillar rows receive the following total and row count
rationale: The Lebanon-timber house has three cedar-pillar rows; the next notice gives forty-five pillars, fifteen per row, with paneling above. The source's hundred-by-fifty-by-thirty house measures and three rows remain unchanged.

relationship: Same-chapter The forty-five pillars and fifteen-per-row notice relates to the three-row house description
rationale: Kings gives forty-five pillars and fifteen per row after describing three cedar-pillar rows in the house. The relationship follows the stated row notices without importing a different row number from another edition.

relationship: Same-chapter Three-tier beams and spaces continue into the doorway arrangement
rationale: The house has three beams and spaces in three tiers; the next unit gives square doorways and spaces with beams and facing doorways in three tiers. Spaces are not independently renamed windows or given unreported dimensions.

relationship: Same-chapter The square doorway-and-space notice retains the preceding three-tier frame
rationale: Square doorways and spaces are fitted with beams in three tiers, following the three-beam and three-tier space notice. The repeated structural descriptions do not supply a new window count or changed tier number.

relationship: Same-chapter The royal-complex sequence distinguishes the pillared porch from the judicial porch notice
rationale: The pillar porch has its own fifty-by-thirty measurements and front structures; the following unit names the throne porch for judgment. The two named porch notices are compared without transferring those measurements to the judgment porch.

relationship: The judicial porch’s stated use corresponds to the king’s recognized judging function
rationale: The throne porch is designated for judgment; the earlier account says Israel recognized God's discernment in Solomon for carrying out justice. It does not place the earlier two-woman case in this later described porch.

relationship: The house for Pharaoh’s daughter relates to the earlier temporary accommodation
rationale: The royal complex includes a house for Pharaoh's daughter, Solomon's wife; the earlier continuation places her in the City of David until the building projects finish. No unreported moving date or exact porch identity is supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter The costly-stone description continues into the specified foundation stones
rationale: The costly-stone account extends from foundation to cornices and the great court; the following unit gives great foundation stones of ten and eight cubits. The relative clause is not independently reassigned to a reconstructed building plan.

relationship: Same-chapter The measured foundation stones continue the preceding costly-stone account
rationale: Ten- and eight-cubit costly great stones form the foundation notice after the account of costly stonework from foundation upward. Their dimensions are not assigned to every other stone or adjoining structure.

relationship: Same-chapter The upper stone-and-cedar notice follows the foundation-course description
rationale: The source adds costly measured unhewn stones and cedars above the preceding foundation-stone account. Its upper work is not automatically given the earlier ten- and eight-cubit foundation measurements.

relationship: The great court’s three stone courses and cedar course have a prior counterpart
rationale: The great court has three unhewn-stone courses and one carved-cedar course; the innermost court earlier has the corresponding three-stone and one-worked-cedar arrangement. Their separate court settings are retained rather than certified as one enclosure.

relationship: Same-chapter The royal-house completion closes the earlier duration notice
rationale: The chapter concludes that Solomon completed his whole house after stating a thirteen-year royal-house construction period. This bookend does not change the separate Lord-house completion and furnishing notices.
